Mr. Chairman, on March 27 I was directing to the house some remarks in regard to recruiting, a subject which was exercising my mind at the time and to which I have given some thought and study since. I have in the meantime made a few observations which I should like to give to the house.
Since returning to Ottawa I have observed something which I think has come under the observation of all members of the house. No later than half-past two this afternoon I passed the most centrally located recruiting station in the city of Ottawa, which, as you will recall, is in the Canadian National railway ticket office on Sparks street. A young man
War Appropriation

was sitting there being interviewed by a private or a corporal. I wondered at the time just what that young lad's feelings and emotions were as he sat beside the man in uniform in that office where ten or twelve clerks were engaged in their daily routine, where there were stenographers, and salesmen selling tickets, and about six people like myself in there buying tickets or making inquiries with regard to transportation. I thought to myself, this is not fair to Canadian youth: to have a young volunteer like this sitting alongside a soldier in uniform, subjected to the gaze of the indifferent and the curious, the interested and the uninterested, and even of those who might be scorning all he was doing at the moment when he was about to dedicate his life to his country. Our young Canadian deserves better of our country and of the cause for which we are fighting. I tried to picture myself in that young man's position twenty or twenty-five years ago, and I wondered what thoughts were passing through his mind as he sat there under the gaze of us all, and the agitation of mind and soul he had experienced possibly in the last twenty-four hours, when he was making up his mind. I imagine that he probably came there looking for advice, sympathy and help in making a momentous decision. A man who comes to volunteer at any of our recruiting offices is entitled at least, in my opinion, to the courtesy of privacy when he is about to make his decision.
Then my mind turned to the officer in charge of the recruiting office and I thought to myself, what is uppermost in his mind? Is he thinking in terms of the young man who has had the courage to come in and offer his life for his country? Or is he thinking in terms of the army and of his job of getting men for the army? I imagine the thought that was uppermost in the recruiting officer's mind was: "Here I have another recruit for the army." I am sure that his success or failure in the eyes of his superior officer depends upon the number of young or middle-aged men who enlist for the Canadian army in that particular recruiting station.
We have heard a lot about selective service. I wonder whether we are applying selective service even in our voluntary enlistment system to-day. That young man may have come from forty or fifty or maybe a hundred miles from Ottawa, where there was no local regiment in his town or village, no unit of the air force or of the navy. He may never have seen a ship at sea or a squadron of planes in the air and may have had little notion in which of the three armed forces he was best qualified to serve his country. It does seem to me that that man is entitled to the best advice and

counsel that our country can afford. It should surely not be left to caprice or chance or even his whim or fancy which of the services he should join. Surely the paramount consideration should be that of public need and necessity. I am afraid that some of the dissatisfaction which exists in our army, navy and air force is due to the fact that men have gone into a particular service without proper advice as to where, by reason of their background, education, training, experience and ability, natural or acquired, they can individually best serve their country. I suggest that the fact that the young man whom I saw this afternoon happened to run into an army recruiting office makes it almost certain that he is now, while I am speaking, a member of his majesty's army. But I wonder whether that is the place where he can best serve his country. If by chance he had stepped into the navy recruiting office, I wonder whether he would not now be a member of the Canadian navy, or if peradventure he had gone into another recruiting office further down the street, I wonder whether he would not now be a member of his majesty's air force. Should such a serious decision as that be left to chance? Are we to look at this thing and allow his fate to be decided solely from the point of view of the needs of the army, or the aggressiveness of the air force regarding recruiting, or by the romantic appeal of the navy? Is chance to be the deciding factor as to which service the young man shall join?
I think we are pretty well convinced now that the time has gone by when men flock to the army in the large numbers witnessed at the outbreak of the war, when the more enthusiastic patriots and some of the unemployed were flocking to the colours. To-day the men offering are possibly more sober-minded or hesitant, thinking of their ties of home and of duty to loved ones who are dependent upon them.
One of the two outstanding things which have been accomplished in Canada in this war has been the creation of the personnel selection service, of which the minister spoke yesterday afternoon in answer to a member representing one of the Winnipeg seats. I was very much interested in what the minister said. That move is very much to be commended. But it does seem to me that the advice, experience and knowledge of these personnel experts, trained medical men and psychologists, could best be applied when the young man first comes forward to offer his services. That is the time he should get counsel and advice as to where, in the opinion of these men, he can best serve. I believe the minister remarked that possibly that branch had not

War Appropriation
been expanded to the extent he wished it to be, because of inability to get sufficient trained men. I wonder whether there is a personnel selection branch in the air force, and similarly for the navy. If not, surely there should be. But why three personnel selection branches? Why three different recruiting depots? Why not one recruiting depot at which Canadian manhood should apply and receive advice from those familiar with the wants and needs of our three services, and be directed into the branch which needs men and in which the particular individual can best serve his king and country? To me the present system of recruiting seems extravagant and shows a lack of cooperation which is reflected down through our three armed forces. It demonstrates failure to appreciate the requirements of the situation. We get the money to finance this war, not through the efforts of the soldiers, the sailors or the airmen, but by relying upon our civilian population and specifically upon men who are skilled in selling victory bonds and promoting the sale of war savings certificates. When it comes to the manufacture of munitions of war, whether they be guns or bullets, uniforms or shoes, we rely upon our trained civilian men, institutions and organizations to provide our armed services with these things. I suggest that the same practice, the same reasoning and the same logic should apply in so far as the recruitment and selection of our manpower are concerned.
In that connection I wish to refer to the work of another department of the army, upon which I think the minister is very much to be congratulated. It has demonstrated more eloquently than anything I can say, through practical results, the theory which I have enunciated regarding the obtaining of men.
In Alberta there are, I believe, at the present time working in cooperation with the army, over 345 civilian agencies. No longer do we have an officer in uniform with a retinue of subordinates travelling from point to point to await the arrival of prospective recruits. In each of these towns and cities the recruiting officer is a civilian, a man of character, reputation, standing and past experience in one of the armed services, and it is generally known or made known to the community that he is there to counsel and advise young men who are entertaining the notion or impressed with the duty of offering their services to their country. This system has worked out remarkably well, and I commend the minister and those associated with him for the success which has attended their efforts in my own province. I should like to
inquire from him how it is working out elsewhere, and whether we cannot have more of that civilian recruiting. I am told, regarding one office in my own city, that a simple advertisement brought in twenty-five responses from tradesmen and mechanics who had seen the classified advertisement in the local papers requesting those interested to present themselves at the office of the assistant civilian director of recruiting services. The response and reaction were splendid, in this respect, that the mechanic, were he young or elderly, came to a private office, was met by a man in civilian clothes, sat down at the desk on terms of perfect freedom and equality with his interviewer, there was not the embarrassment of a private citizen talking to a man who was already in the army, and counsel and advice were given without regard to any particular branch of the service. I know that one man, a diesel expert working in a country garage, was sent to a place east of Calgary, where a diesel expert was urgently needed in the army. I know that another applicant, who had served his apprenticeship on the Clyde and was an experienced shipbuilder, was not sent to the army or the navy or the air force, but was advised that he could best serve his king and country in the shipbuilding yards at Vancouver. And so on down the line.
I should welcome a statement from the minister as to what, if any, cooperation or coordination there is, with respect to recruiting, between the three armed services. I wonder how many hon. members are familiar with the situation of the young man who has volunteered his services for the air force and, although , a period of three to six months has intervened, has not been called and is still carrying on in civilian life. We were told some months ago that the Department of National Defence for Naval Services had at that time a waiting list of 4,000 or 5,000. Where is the need to-day? Is it certain that these 5,000 men waiting to be called to the navy, these 10,000 or 20,000 waiting to be called to the air force, can best serve their country in those services? Who knows? Has anybody examined these men having regard to their potential capacities and abilities, in order to ascertain whether some who have volunteered for the navy could not better serve their country in the tanks or in the artillery? What is it that decides where a man shall go? Is it the needs of the country, or his training, or experience and background; or merely his whim or preference; or is it, who "gets to him" first?
Another question in my mind is, what cooperation is there between the three armed
War Appropriation

forces in Canada in so far as their training is concerned? I have yet to hear of any place where the army and the air force are carrying out their training in cooperation with each other. That may have been done, but I was wondering, because I had not seen or heard that it had been done; and yet we are -all aware that in every great battle fought so far in this war it has been the close cooperation or lack of it between the air force, the artillery and the infantry that has spelled success or failure as the case may be. I would welcome a statement from the minister, if he is at liberty to give one, as to the extent to which our two or three forces-because we have three now-are cooperating in training. What does the airman know about the ground tactics and operations of the infantryman. Is there any cooperation as between the navy and air force so far as training is concerned?
I should like to have a statement from the minister on another point, because I have had this thrown at me on two or three occasions, that once a man is in the navy he must perforce stay there regardless of his personal desires or training or ability, that he cannot go from the navy to the air force or from the air force to the infantry. I do not know whether that is well-founded or not, but only yesterday I received a letter from one of my constituents indicating that he was not permitted to transfer from one force to another. I would welcome a statement on this point.
Another question that has disturbed me a little is this. I should like to know if the minister is at liberty to tell us what, if any, has been the number of desertions from the Canadian army attendant upon departure from Canada for overseas, and what disposition, if any, is made of those who have deserted, if and when found. I should like to know whether or not desertion is a common practice or whether the department have knowledge of any extensive dismissals of persons from the army, the navy or the air force for any crime record or absence without leave, and whether such persons have gone to another district and reenlisted in one of the armed services. I am led to believe that there is a considerable number. Far be it from me to spread rumours, but I should like to know as a matter of fact what action is taken with regard to such persons.
There is one other question that is pertinent so far as the financing of the army and of the war effort is concerned. I should like to know with respect to the permanent staff whether they are still eligible for pensions. I believe that in the ordinary course of events they are entitled to pension after twenty-one years in the service. What happens to a man who is a sergeant or a corporal in the permanent staff

and who since the outbreak of war, has become a major or a colonel-and I believe that has happened. Will he retire on pension at the colonel's rating, or will he retire at the status which he had at the time of the outbreak of war?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I agree with the member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) that the minister has been very patient and thorough in his answers to the committee on questions that have been brought to his attention. I wish to come back for a moment to the question of dependents' allowances in order to bring another category to his attention, because in my opinion this category is getting anything but justice. I refer now to the man who enlists and has a housekeeper. The reason why I bring this to the minister's attention is that I thoroughly discussed at least two cases with the allowance board, but I have not to date received any redress. I wish to submit one case in particular. The mother died in 1931, and the daughter at that time had to leave school, become the housekeeper and care for the rest of the family. The father enlisted fourteen or fifteen months ago. The family is receiving no income with the exception of the assigned pay of the father.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Is the daughter still
keeping house?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, and has been continuously since 1931. A younger brother at the present time is coming out of a sanatorium after undergoing treatment for tuberculosis, and on the 1st of May I received another letter asking whether something could not be done. This is not an isolated case. There are several of this kind, to my knowledge, and I presume there are a good many of them throughout the country. I have written to the minister to-day on the subject, and I leave this case specifically with him.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What reason did the board give for not making the allowance on account of the daughter who was in the position of housekeeper?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The only reason the dependent has received is that she does not come under the regulations within the meaning of "dependent", because she is a housekeeper, and is a daughter and not the wife of the man. That is the attitude they have taken right through the case.
Another thought I should like to leave with the minister is with regard to boys under age who enlist. I know that the regulations definitely state that no boy shall

War Appropriation
go overseas unless he is nineteen, but there are many boys who are enlisting by covering up their ages. The reason for that is that in some instances the parents cannot keep them at school in the higher grades. The books cost a lot of money. Moreover, they cannot get employment when they leave school; they go to a recruiting officer and say they are nineteen; after they have been in for six or eight months taking training and are ready to proceed overseas, the parents produce a certificate, and the boy is taken out of the army. The point I make is that the boy is relegated back to the streets. There is no employment for him, particularly in the part of the country from which I come, and I am aware of many cases of this kind. Has the department ever given any consideration to the establishment of a boys' brigade or battalion such as we had during the last war?
Instead of wasting the training that has been given, sending them back to the street whence they came, would it not be better to place them in a trade school and give them some training for employment in industry which would serve a purpose now and fit them for something after the war? Many of these boys are going overseas at that age, and I know that, as happened during the last war, many of them who went over are weeded out. A boy seventeen years of age is not much good on active service; he is too young. I have a case in point to-day, a letter received from a father who has one boy eighteen years of age in England. The second boy, who is only seventeen, has now gone over. The father made application to the Department of National Defence, and he encloses to me a letter signed for the Adjutant, Captain MacCallum, dated April 10, giving him the assurance that this boy would not proceed overseas until he was nineteen years of age.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is the younger one?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That is right. The next thing he knows is he is informed that the boy is in England, regardless of the letter of the adjutant. The question of boys under age is something [DOT]to which I think the department should give serious consideration.
Another category about which something should be done is that of men weeded out of the army. I have seen many discharge certificates where men and boys were discharged by reason of being underweight, with no particular disability. Another discharge certificate would read, "Does not come up to the required physical standards." Again no particular disability. With regard to most
people discharged by reason of being underweight, this is due to lack of proper food. Instead of sending these people back to the street-certainly no industry wants a man in that physical condition-if a period of training and proper feeding were given in a camp, the chances are that within a few months they would meet the required physical standards.
I thought these three points were worth bringing to the attention of the minister because I know there are many cases such as I have described.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In reference to the eighteen-year old boy, if he is eighteen I am instructed that he is kept overseas unless his parents desire him to come home. As to the one seventeen years old, the general rule is to discharge him. I must say that unless he applies or makes it noticeable what his age is and if he wants to stay in the army, I do not think he is "turfed" to use the army expression. But a case of this kind where the adjutant of the battalion told him he would not be sent overseas is to my mind absolutely unexplainable. There obviously it was accepted that he was seventeen and therefore he should not have gone overseas. Has my hon. friend written me about that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
With regard to the nutritional eases, I am obliged to the committee for two or three instances becauses they all aid in discovering a general trend. I cannot understand the medical board discharging a man on the ground of underweight or that he does not come up to the required standard. I understand that discharges should be specific, indicating what the disability is. With regard to nutrition my hon. friend is perfectly right, and it wTas made clear in the statement by the Prime Minister in connection with man-power. He pointed out that it is and has been standard practice for the army to accept men for service who required only dental treatment, provision of glasses, or nutritional improvement, and they are to be given them. In the face of that statement of policy, I do not understand why a man is discharged for being underweight unless he has some functional or organic disability which means that he cannot be brought up to weight by proper nutrition. I shall certainly inquire into that case.
My hon, friend mentioned another case, the matter of dependents' allowances; I shall look into that. It sounds as if there should be an allowance for the daughter who is keeping house, and why it is not granted we shall have to find out from the dependents' allowance board. My hon. friend suggested that the regulations did not cover it, but I cannot
War Appropriation

believe that; I am satisfied they do cover the case of someone taking the place of the mother.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It has been a matter of correspondence with the department, the allowance board, for the last five or six months.

I think it was the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Edwards) who spoke of the matter of transfers. There is no right of transfer as between any of the arms of the service. That is, after a man is in as a member of one arm he cannot as of right ask transfer to some other. The procedure is that he applies to his commanding officer for transfer to the other service, and the considerations which influence the commanding officer in granting or refusing that request are obviously (1) how long the man has been training, how much time has been spent fitting him for the particular arm of the service in which he is, and (2) his usefulness in connection with that arm of the service. I think reasonable endeavour is made to meet his desires, but obviously if you had a man highly trained for a year or two as a signaller in a particular unit, the commanding officer would feel reluctant to let him go to some other arm of the service where perhaps that training would not be so valuable.

Does the man there have some option, or must he go where he is put? I know an instance of a man who understood he was going to the ordnance from the very beginning, but he was put into the artillery. He did not want to go there. He had a bent for the ordnance. I am not sure that the case has been settled yet. I have been trying to help him fulfil his desire, but I realize that there are two sides to the question. Possibly he is not fitted for the ordnance. Someone higher up would have to make the decision, but there ought to be some flexibility in a case like that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is sometimes given on compassionate grounds?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Sometimes that is done on compassionate grounds; families may be located at one place or another, and for the time being the man may be allowed to go to a certain camp or centre. I am speaking of the army, not the air force, about which my hon. friend really is asking. I must say that we cannot take into consideration very much the compassionate grounds of which my hon. friend speaks. Obviously, since there are now training centres all over Canada, men would like to go to the particular training centre nearest their homes. That cannot be done, and veiy often it is obviously desirable that they should go somewhere else, in order to gain experience away from home.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Some months ago, according to an announcement in the press and, if my memory serves me aright, an announcement also in this house, provision was made for the issuing of discharge buttons, or at least buttons which would indicate that a person had been rejected after having applied for enlistment in the active service forces. I was wondering to what extent these rejection buttons had been issued and what were the regulations covering their distribution.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There are two buttons available. One is the discharge button; that is to say, a man who has enlisted for general service and who later has been discharged, receives one type of button. The other is the applicant for enlistment button. The adjutant-general cannot tell me the number issued so far, but they are available on application.
War Appropriation

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In connection with these applications for enlistment, if a man enlists for any particular branch of the service and is rejected, is a button issued by virtue of that application, or does it have to be a general enlistment?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Could the minister also give the committee some information with respect to the army train which is going across Canada at the moment, as to how long it has been in operation, and as to the personnel accompanying that train across the country?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It started on February 3 and, as I remember it, went first to central Canada, then east, and then west. I think it is due back very soon now. This personnel were changed in the various parts of the country to which the train went. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Was the purpose of the train to stimulate recruiting?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
To stimulate recruiting
and interest in the army. It was simply taking the army to Canadians at a time when we could not have demonstrations which would bring Canadians to the army. As the hon. gentleman knows, from time to time people have asked for armoured demonstrations. We have had detachments go to various places and give these demonstrations, but that could not be done in the winter. So it was suggested that we should use the railway instead of using the roads. In addition, I believe one car was devoted to the victory loan campaign, and part of one car to the Red Cross as well.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I should like to ask a question as a matter of information, because I have received a great many wires and complaints about it. Who advised the stops that were made in British Columbia?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I cannot tell my hon.
friend that, but, as far as I know, I do not believe there was anyone in this house who did not advise stops. As a matter of fact, the adjutant-general tells me that a real endeavour was made to have stops at all

places possible, where there might be interest shown. He says further that one factor which governed was the physical factor, that is, the length of the railway sidings at the various points, which decided whether or not the train could be accommodated there. So the railways had to be consulted in deciding where the stops should be made.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Would the
minister be kind enough after the dinner recess, or at some other convenient time, to make a general statement in connection with the recommendations brought in last year with regard to an interdepartmental committee functioning as between the different branches of the service, and so on? I think the minister knows to what I refer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There are two points I should like to clear up. The first is whether or not men in category Cl are being called up under the national mobilization regulations. In view of that fact I should like the minister to explain why these men are not entitled to buttons.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend may not think it is a good reason, but the adjutant-general tells me that the man in category E is the only man who is almost definitely out. An E-category man may improve, but there is very little chance of it. There is much more chance that a C-eategory man may improve, and so far the button has not been issued to men in C category, because the time may come when they may be eligible for enlistment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
By virtue of the medical
qualifications being reduced?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: By virtue of a change in their category. However, the matter is still under advisement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But that man is required to sign an undertaking that if the class in which he is placed eventually comes within the category of men eligible for active service, he will submit himself for further examination. So there is no reason why a Cl man should not be given a button.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite right, and it even goes further than that. As a matter of fact, the regulations under which the badges are issued provide that there is a right to recall the badge itself if subsequently the category in which the applicant

War Appropriation
is placed becomes a category which should be called up. As I indicated, however, the matter is still under advisement.
My hon. friend was good enough to send his other question to me. That was whether any men in the medical category Cl have been called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act, as the regulations are administered. I think that is the question. Of course my hon. friend understands that under the general regulations any category could be called, but, as I understand the situation, under the instructions issued to the medical officers, at the present time the only men who are being sent in, who are being forwarded to the training centres after having been, examined by the medical officer in the particular town, are men who have passed that medical officer as A. If they get into the training centre and, after being examined by the army officer, turn out to be B, but not lower, they are retained in the training centre. The specific answer to my hon. friend's question is that C category are not called in the sense that C category are returned home if, on examination by the local medical officer, they turn out to be in that category.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the
Prime Minister announced the new orders in council providing for the national selective service programme he stated that provision was being made for the calling up of aliens, and similar statements have appeared at different times in the press. For example, we find in "Canada's War Record" of May, 1942, this statement:
Liability for military service is being extended to all residents in Canada whether citizens or not.
There have also been statements in the press to the effect that the calling up of men who are not British subjects would have to wait for the conclusion of international negotiations with the countries of which those aliens are citizens. Would the minister tell us when these aliens will be called up and in what way they will be used by the armed forces? It would also be interesting if the minister could tell us what groups of aliens are to be called up.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That matter has not been settled yet. It is in the hands of the Department of External Affairs.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
What is the situation with
regard to Canadians in other countries? Why is it necessary for Canada to enter into an agreement with each of the governments ' concerned?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Because I think each
government as a matter of international law reserves its rights with regard to other nationals in its own country. But my hon. friend is getting me beyond my depth, and I do not propose to go into that matter at any length. I can only say that the matter is under consideration and, I believe, under negotiation by the Department of External Affairs at the present time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In what way will these
aliens be used by the Canadian armed forces? Will they be put, for example, into the armed forces, or are they to be used on road work, or has the government some other plan in mind regarding them? Surely the government must have had some plan in mind when it decided to call up these men.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think the decision was
to open negotiations with regard to calling the men up. I cannot forecast in what way they will be used. So far as I know they will probably be used in the same way as others who are called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Go right into the armed
forces?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is what I say, so far as I know. I have no reason for thinking otherwise, except that they might be used for any other purpose for which they could be called up under the act.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is the present situation with regard to United States citizens in our Canadian forces?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There are two phases.to
it, as my hon. friend knows. One phase is that United States citizens in Canada were given a certain option to go back to their own forces, if the option was exercised by a certain date, and that date has been extended. There was a reciprocal provision with regard to Canadians in the United States forces. The other matter, the calling up of aliens in Canada, is still under consideration by the Department of External Affairs, along with the other question which my hon. friend mentioned which has to do with all aliens.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Press dispatches yesterday
stated that representatives of the armed forces of the United States would land at Saint John on May 5, which is to-day, apparently to make arrangements for giving United
War Appropriation

States citizens who are serving in the Canadian forces an opportunity to transfer to United States forces. Can the minister tell us anything about that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is part of the agreement which has been or is being concluded between the United States and ourselves. The parties who are coming here are coming for the purpose of meeting, at various points across Canada, United States citizens in our own services who have elected to go to the United States, and arranging for their medical examination and details with regard to transportation and so forth.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: How many men in the Canadian forces will be affected?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No one has any figures on that so far as I know. I think I stated some time ago-it was just a general statement and was not made in connection with these negotiations-that there were from six to seven thousand United States citizens in the Canadian army. I also stated that including staff pilots there were

I am speaking from memory-at that time some 2,300 in the Canadian air force. That was some time ago, and I have no doubt that there are quite a number more who have joined the air force since.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Are not friendly aliens in
Canada subject now to call by their own governments or by their governments in exile in other countries?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Oh, yes, they are subject to call under their own laws, but the Canadian government under international law does not necessarily assist in the enforcement of those laws.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But they are notified by their own government?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
At an earlier stage of this debate I raised the question of easier transportation facilities for the men on active service and suggested that the minister might consider calling together a small committee of men in the ranks of the armed forces for the purpose of advising in connection with some of the matters to which I then referred.
It. is along that line I want to say a word further to-night. I am advised that in the newly organized United States army they have a system which I bring to the attention of the^ minister with some reluctance because it is not likely that he will pay any more attention to his civilian critics than we are justly entitled to but I hope this example 
may not be overlooked in the new disciplinary arrangements which the Canadian army has in mind. In an effort towards what is regarded as the democratization of the United States army, 3,000 questionnaires, each containing 118 questions, have been sent to a selected number of men in the ranks. In other words, these men have been asked to give essential opinions regarding several important aspects of the army's work. One of these questions asks how the services of the man in the armed forces may be made more efficient; another invites suggestions as to improvement of the army in efficiency, discipline and other respects. This approach to the troops may be said to follow out in a more comprehensive way the suggestion which I originally made of a select committee consisting of men in the ranks. Perhaps the reference of army matters to the "man underneath" is not so unorthodox a procedure as upon its face it may seem to be. In the formulation of future policies the minister might give some consideration to this suggestion which comes from the United States army itself. May I ask whether the department has any plans in mind which would lead to that objective?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, we have an organization which was set up comparatively recently; we call it a special services directorate. It deals with just such matters as my hon. friend has mentioned

shall I say, matters of morale; that is part of it, on matters both inside and outside the army, suggestions either from civilians or from soldiers to improve the service of the individual, to employ his capacities more usefully, and also for the improvement of the army generally.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Has the machinery actually been set in operation?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There has been a questionnaire.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: When my hon. friend says "machinery", no questionnaires have been sent out along the lines he has suggested, but other steps have been taken to secure opinions and views with regard to such matters.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I wish to submit to the minister one or two questions which will not take long to ask but may take longer to answer. Are the fourth, sixth, seventh and eighth divisions up to strength? Is each of these divisions fully officered? Is each of them fully equipped? If any of them are not fully up to strength, fully officered or

War Appropriation
fully equipped, when does the minister expect to have them up to strength, fully officered and fully equipped? Who are the officers commanding these four divisions?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I thought the hon. member asked about the fourth, sixth and seventh.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The fourth, sixth, seventh and eighth-if they have been named. If they have not been named, does the minister expect that they will be named soon? Can he inform us also of the names of the officers of the brigades in those four divisions?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It will not take me long to answer the first question, with regard to the matter of strengths of the fourth, sixth, seventh and eighth divisions. I am sure my hon. friend will not expect me to give that information. The matter of the strengths of divisions and of units is not one on which I would make a public statement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I did not ask for the
numerical strength; I meant, were they up to strength? We know that they have an establishment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It is the same thing. I do not think I should make a statement about that.
With regard to the names of the commanding officers. The name of the commanding officer of the fourth division is Major General F. L. Worthington, who was in command of the first army tank brigade in Britain, and who was brought back to command that division.
With regard to the officers commanding the sixth and seventh divisions, announcement will be made very soon. The eighth division is not far enough advanced in mobilization to name an officer commanding at the present time. Did my hon. friend ask another question?	,

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Brigades.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I asked about the equipment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The same consideration applies to the question of equipment. I would not make an answer with regard to the equipment of an individual division.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Well, the names of the officers commanding the brigades comprising the divisions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The officers in command of the two armoured brigades of the fourth division are Brigadier Burns and Brigadier Thomas. Brigadier Hyde is in command of the support group of the fourth division.
With regard to the sixth division, Brigadier Leclaire, Brigadier Colquhoun and Brigadier Martin are the three officers commanding brigades. Brigade commanders for the seventh division have not yet been named.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
One day last week I raised with the minister the question of the policy the government is following in connection with men who were on farms on the 23rd of March, when the Prime Minister announced the government's policy. I mentioned a number of cases. I have in mind one in particular where the man was on the farm until the 1st of April. I have received to-day a letter from the officer commanding in Regina to the effect that in view of the fact that this man's case was heard on the 27th of February, 1942, and he was granted postponement to April 1 and it was definitely marked "final; no action can be taken by this department". A letter dated May 1, from the young man informs me that they have 300 acres of land ready to seed and they have not been able to get any help. Could the minister make some statement in this connection in view of order in council 2251, which starts as follows:
Whereas the Minister of National War Services and the Acting Minister of Labour report that there is a growing shortage of agricultural labour and that it is necessary for the effective prosecution of the war to take steps to stabilize employment in agriculture. . . .
Have these orders been relayed to the different officers concerned, and will the minister explain the relationship between his department and the Department of National War Services? The Department of National War Services informed me over the telephone that they have no further jurisdiction after a man has been called up by the army, and the officer in charge informs me that they have no jurisdiction because the Department of National War Services on February 27, before this order was passed, had reached certain conclusions. Could the minister make a statement as to whether some definite policy can be announced?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Did I understand that some decision had been made by the board on February 27, granting postponement or the reverse?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Until the 1st of April, but he was called on the 1st of April.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is the situation now? Is there a further application for postponement?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes. The man has made his application to the officer commanding. The officer reports that a decision
War Appropriation

was reached on this date in February and that they cannot do anything about it. The man is still in the army, although he was actually on the farm on March 23 when the Prime Minister announced the policy that was to apply to all men then engaged in agriculture.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: One hesitates to deal with facts that are a little complicated; but it sounded to me as if- the man, when he was called for the 1st of April, should have appeared before the board and asked for postponement on the ground that he was engaged in agriculture on March 23. He should have made his claim then. The rule is that if he does, and shows that he was wholly or partly engaged in agriculture at that time, the burden is on someone else, I suppose the army authorities or the Department of National War Services, itself, to show that he was still, even though wholly or mainly engaged in agriculture, not essential thereto. I do not know why he has not made that application. Perhaps he has. If he has not made that application and has gone into the service he may still apply to the commanding officer, who will refer the application to the board through the district officer commanding. My hon. friend refers to a particular case and I shall ascertain what has been done. This is one of those cases that would appear to bridge over the time of the zero date when men were frozen in agricultural pursuits. If the man is in the army and my hon. friend will send me his name I will endeavour to see what has been done about the matter. What the. army has done is to agree to accept the recommendation of the boards which have been constituted under the National War Services Act in connection with applications of this kind, subject to military exigencies, as my hon. friend will understand.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I wish the
minister would elaborate this matter. There has been a good deal of confusion with reference to it. I do not know that his department is as much responsible as the Department of National War Services, but my time during the Easter recess was almost entirely taken up with this problem. Nearly 1,000 men in Saskatchewan were due to begin training on April 9, but were on farms on March 23. I got in touch with the Department of National War Services, as many others did, and we were told that these men should report because their call came prior to March 23 and that therefore they had to report, but that if they reported they could make application to be allowed at least to go home for spring

seeding. Most of the men got in touch with me and I passed that advice on. I told them that they must report and then make application for leave to go home for spring seeding.
That, however, has raised another problem, and I wish the minister would make a clarifying statement either now or later in the session. As soon as it was announced that some provision was to be made to give soldiers leave for spring seeding, scores of farmers wrote asking me and, I have no doubt, other hon. members as well, what steps they should take to have itheir boys given leave to come home for spring seeding, and this came particularly from men up in years farming large tracts of land. I did not feel personally that I ought to take the time of the minister or of his deputy, both of whom have a great many other things to do, by referring individual cases to them. What I did was to point out to these men the procedure which their sons must follow. I told them that they should apply to the commanding officer and that the application would be forwarded to the Department of National War Services and be decided upon. In many cases that worked satisfactorily. Some of these men have been given leave to go home and put in the crop, but I am now receiving letters in which soldiers say that when they go to the commanding officer they are told that he knows nothing of such a provision; that it must be a rumour, and therefore nothing is done about it. In some cases the application is accepted reluctantly and the men hear no more about the matter. Such communications come in every day. I hesitate to take up the time of the minister with these individual cases, but the matter is pressing so far as these people are concerned.
The other day I had a letter from the secretary of a municipality giving a list of elderly men in his municipality who will not be able to put in a crop this year if they cannot get help, and they cannot get help in the surrounding communities. The boys have not been able to get leave for seeding. This is what happens. If a young man happens to belong to a unit where the commanding officer understands the situation and is sympathetic, the boy gets leave, in some cases, for six weeks. The hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) mentioned a young man who had been given six months leave, but there are few such cases. On a neighbouring farm, however, there happens to' be another man whose son also made application and he has never heard anything about the matter. It is difficult to explain to two farmers why one gets six weeks, or six months as the case may be, and the other no leave. I imagine the difference is in the commanding officers,

War Appropriation
but 'the people on the farms do not think so. They think one man must have more influence than the other.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It must be the government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes. I wish the minister would make a clarifying statement with regard to applications for leave. If the commanding officers clearly understand that provision has been made that the application must be forwarded immediately to the war services board, individual cases will, I believe, be dealt with. Could the minister make such a clarifying statement either to the committee or to the commanding officers across the country?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If Hitler comes he will give us all leave to be slaves.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend is under a misapprehension when he speaks of a provision having been made. The only provision which has been made is the provision that when an application is made for compassionate leave-not for seeding, but for leave under special circumstances-the commanding officer makes a recommendation, whatever it may be, and passes it on to the district officer commanding, who sends it to the board, and when the board makes a recommendation the regulations require that that recommendation shall be accepted, unless the exigencies of the service are such as to make it inadvisable to do so. But that is not leave for seeding. That is where the misapprehension arises. I tried to make it clear the other night that the army cannot spare a man for seeding, any more than can the air force or the navy, and that we should not be asked to take on two jobs. These units are being mobilized as rapidly as they can be; there is urgent need for them, particularly in some parts of the country, and we feel that we cannot agree to any policy which means the wholesale release of men who are in the middle of training to go back for seeding.
If there are individual cases of hardship, cases in which compassionate leave should be granted and which the boards think are proper cases, they are considered by the board. When my hon. friend says the commanding officer knew of no such provision, I think he must mean that the commanding officer knew of no such provision for granting leave for seeding, because I think all commanding officers know that we have delegated to the boards under the Department of National War Services the discretion in connection with proper cases of application for compassionate leave. That is probably not very satisfying to my hon. friends, and
particularly to those who are writing and who apparently have the idea that there is actual provision for leave for seeding, but that is only in connection with depots and some home guard establishments, and I do not think it applies to any of the units to which my hon. friend refers, or to the training centres.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They apply particularly to young men in training under the National Resources Mobilization Act, a great many of whom have been in for but a short time. When I say "provision for seeding" I must not be misunderstood. I am aware that no general provision was made to allow any soldier to go home for seeding, but I think there was some provision that if a man could show that he was absolutely required at home and that those at home could not carry on the spring operations without him, some consideration would be given.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not think those considerations were mentioned. It was purely a procedural order in council that was passed. The idea was to get away from the idea that the army made the full decision; that is, to give people opportunity to make a special case under special circumstances, but I do not think it had reference to seeding or putting in a crop or agricultural operations alone. I think it had reference to compassionate leave.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
